question: Was the deportation of 1915 a wartime relocation or the destruction of a people, and what does the free record hold about who decided it and how many died?
claims: The dispatches of the Ottoman Empire's ally and of a neutral, written while it ran, record measures extended beyond any war zone, decided in the capital, with the eradication of the Armenians as their purpose; the two ambassadors agree on 5 points of 6.

The count of the dead is a set of counts with their producers, from the American Committee's 450,000 to the White House's 1,500,000, and the interior ministry's own tally of 1917 counted about a quarter of the Armenians in its own 1914 column, fewer than a quarter of the census total its notes print.

The Turkish state's case is held in its own words and tested: its war-zone claim is contradicted by its ally's record, its claim that no plan existed is qualified on archives this record cannot reach, and its count of Muslim dead cannot be tested here at all.

sentences.text: On 24 May 1915 the Allied governments told the Sublime Porte that they would hold personally responsible for “these new crimes of Turkey against humanity and civilization” every member of the Ottoman government implicated in the massacres.
On 7 July 1915 the German ambassador, the ally's, reported to his chancellor that the relocation showed the government “pursuing its purpose of eradicating the Armenian race from the Turkish Empire”.

On 10 July the American ambassador, a neutral's, telegraphed that the measures were “purely arbitrary and directed from Constantinople in the name of military necessity, often in districts where no military operations are likely to take place”.
The government's own pamphlet of 1916 called the same measures a transfer of the Armenians from the military zones to secure the rear of the army.
This thesis asks whether the deportation was the relocation the state named or the destruction the ambassadors named, and what the free record holds about who decided it and how many died.
It makes three claims.
First, that the ally's file and the neutral's file agree, on 5 of 6 points, on measures extended beyond any war zone, decided in the capital, and aimed at the eradication of a people.

Second, that the count of the dead is a set of counts with their producers and is stated here as that, and that the interior ministry's own tally of 1917 counted about a quarter of the Armenians in its own column for 1914, and fewer than a quarter of the census total in its notes.
Third, that the Turkish state's account is held here in its own words and tested against its ally's record, and that where the test needs the Ottoman archives, this record says so and stops.
The primary record this thesis holds is of five producers, and the reader should know whose paper each verdict stands on.
The American file is the ambassador's telegrams of 1915 as the Department of State printed them, with the telegram of 16 July read in a facsimile.

The German file is the Foreign Office's own reports, read in the transcription an online edition publishes from the Berlin archive, in the original German with the edition's English translation held beside it as a separate work.
The British compilation of 1916 is a belligerent government's, and its documents are American, Armenian, German and Swiss witnesses; its historical summary is Toynbee's own.
The Ottoman state speaks here through its pamphlet of 1916, in French, and through the interior minister's tally of 1917, read in an English edition.
The survivors speak through a narrative an Armenian of Moush recorded on 25 July 1915, printed first in the Armenian journal Van-Tosp and reprinted by the British ministry.
The other survivor voice held is a memoir written up for American readers.

What the free record refused is listed by name in the ledger's gaps, and the largest are the Ottoman archives, the court-martial verdict of 1919 as gazetted, the Strasbourg judgment on the word and every standard monograph of the last 20 years, each behind a paywall or a challenge page.

The scholarship is therefore held through open articles in French, German, Turkish and English and through the monographs' titles only, and the Turkish state's own archival case is known here through the historians who describe its fonds, not through the fonds.
The one Turkish-language article held argues the state's reading, that the Armenians were subjected to relocation for an internal security problem.
No Armenian-language scholarship is held: the Yerevan articles are read in English, and the only Armenian on the page is the Republic's declaration.

Four further gaps are named here because the page leans on what they hold: the Whitaker report to the United Nations Sub-Commission, served only as a scan without text; the stenographic record of the Tehlirian trial; Lemkin's book; and the Near East Relief history that the orphans photograph comes from.
Where two counts disagree they are set out below as counts with their producers, and the thesis states none of them as the number.

sections.title: 1. What the two ambassadors wrote in the same week

sentences.text: On 31 May 1915 the German ambassador telegraphed that Enver Pasha meant to close a large number of Armenian schools, suppress Armenian newspapers, forbid Armenian postal correspondence and settle in Mesopotamia every family from the insurgent Armenian centres that was not wholly beyond reproach, and that he urgently asked Germany not to stay his hand.

On 17 June the same ambassador reported that the banishment “is not only motivated by military considerations”, because the interior minister, Talaat Bey, had told an embassy official “that the Porte is intent on taking advantage of the World War in order to make a clean sweep of internal enemies”.
A few days later the Armenian Patriarch told the same official that the measures were intended “to expel them from Turkey or rather to eradicate them altogether”.

sentences.text: On 7 July the ambassador wrote that until 14 days before, the expulsion had been limited to the provinces nearest the eastern theatre and parts of Adana, and that the Porte had since extended it to Trebizond, Mamuret-ul-Aziz and Sivas, “even though these parts of the country are not threatened by any enemy invasion for the time being”.

About 30,000 people in the Vilayet of Trebizond alone were to be deported through Erzincan to Mesopotamia, the route ran through the Kurdish district of Dersim, and the Vali of Trebizond declared openly that he could guarantee the transport only as far as Erzincan; the consul at Erzurum put the Armenians killed on the road to Harput at 3,000.

The same report records the memorandum the ambassador handed to the Grand Vizier on the 4th, approving deportation only insofar as military considerations required it, and states why it was written: to be able to answer later accusations by Germany's enemies of complicity in the rigorous Turkish measures.

Three days later the American ambassador telegraphed Washington that reports from widely scattered districts indicated “systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations”, that the measures were “not in response to popular or fanatical demand”, that “Most of the sufferers are innocent and have been loyal to Ottoman Government”, and that the German embassy would, he believed, “simply content itself with giving advice and a formal protest probably intended for record and to cover itself from future responsibility”.
He added the consul at Harput's line, “There seems to be a systematic plan to crush the Armenian race”.
Neither report cites the other; one government was the Porte's ally, the other neutral.

sentences.text: On 16 July the neutral telegraphed that “it appears that a campaign of race extermination is in progress under a pretext of reprisal against rebellion.” On the same day his German colleague forwarded his consul at Samsun's report, which held that “a great Armenian conspiracy was excellently organised in the whole of Anatolia” and, in the next paragraph, that the countermeasures involved “nothing less than the destruction or enforced Islamization of a whole people, whose relatives for the greatest part did not even participate in the revolutionary movement”.
The German record holds both the conspiracy and the destruction in one file, and this thesis quotes both.

sentences.text: The German administrator at Erzurum wrote on 5 August 1915 that the inhabitants of the plains of Erzurum and Passin, by then “only women, children and old men”, were driven out of their villages towards Mesopotamia, that on the way to Erzincan they were attacked, robbed and killed by Kurds and Turkish volunteers, and that “Between 10 and 20,000 people were probably killed, but the government's figures fall between only 3 and 4,000.” He judged that a measure “which might have been justified militarily and politically in some ways, has turned into a campaign of revenge, destruction and robbery”, and that in the Vilayet of Erzurum “neither weapons nor compromising documents were found”.

A landowning bey of standing, whose guest he had been, told him that the earlier massacres had been fights among men, and that now, against the Koran, innocent women and children were being murdered, not by a crowd in a passion but systematically and on the order of the government, the Committee.

The consul at Aleppo reported on 27 July that bodies had floated past Rumkaleh, Biredjik and Djerablus on the Euphrates “for a total of 25 days”, bound together “two by two, back to back”, which he read as killing by the authorities and not by bands.

A woman from the village of Kheiban, one of the deported of the Moush district, told her story to an Armenian of Moush then in hiding, who wrote it down on 25 July 1915 for the Armenian journal Van-Tosp, from which the British compilation reprinted it: the women and children of village after village were gathered into “a company of 8,000 to 10,000 people”, the old and the weak “were killed”, the guards “Very often they violated eight or ten-year-old girls”, and “Our company moved on slowly, leaving heaps of corpses behind”.
By the boundary of the Ginj district, she said, “our number was diminished by half”; at a river the guards ordered them to cross, and many obeyed.
Aurora Mardiganian's memoir describes the first dawn of her convoy, when Kurdish riders came down on the camp, gathered the animals and walked among the women to pick out the young ones.

On 11 August the American ambassador wrote that the people of Ada Bazar, Izmid and Bardizag, “some 50 miles from Constantinople”, would be “herded like cattle into the arid and hostile wastes of the interior, where the greater number, possibly excepting those who in desperation embrace Mohammedanism, will doubtless perish by murder or slow starvation”.
On 3 September he telegraphed that “Destruction of Armenian race in Turkey is progressing rapidly”.

sentences.text: The Ottoman government's pamphlet of 1916 holds that the commander of the Imperial Army, finding the Armenians making common cause with the enemy, was forced to order the transfer southward of the Armenian element in localities considered military zones, to secure the rear of his troops.

It describes the measures as preventive rather than repressive, taken after the dissolution of the Armenian committees, and states that during their application the Armenians were at times the victims of regrettable abuses and violence, which it calls inevitable given the indignation of the Muslim population.
Ahmed Rüstem Bey, formerly ambassador at Washington, argued in his book that the Entente's charge of extermination was absurd because so many Ottoman Armenians survived.

The Republic's foreign ministry holds the same line: that the government relocated the Armenian population in or near the war zone, that some Armenians away from the front were included, and that no authentic evidence of a premeditated plan to kill Armenians exists.

The ally's file tests the first of those claims and contradicts it: the extension to Trebizond, Mamuret-ul-Aziz and Sivas was reported by the German ambassador on 7 July as reaching provinces threatened by no invasion, and the consul at Samsun on the Black Sea reported the expulsion order as “apparently valid for all Anatolian Vilayets”.

The second claim, that no authentic evidence of a plan exists, is tested here against the interior minister's own words as the German embassy recorded them and against the two ambassadors' independent readings, and no further: the Ottoman archives and the court-martial verdict of 1919 could not be read free, and a verdict on documents this record does not hold would be a guess.
The interior minister's own report is held, and it counts.

sentences.text: Toynbee wrote in the British compilation that the first step was the number of Armenians in the Ottoman frontiers when the deportations began, and that “there are no independent foreign estimates of this on record”: the Patriarchate's enquiry of 1912 placed it as high as 2,100,000 and the Ottoman government's latest returns at 1,100,000 and no more.
He took 1,600,000 provisionally and wrote that the true figure lay between that and 2,000,000.

Tatoyan, from the Yerevan museum, sets the two official series side by side, 1,294,851 in the Ottoman figures of 1914 against 2,026,700 in the Patriarchate's, and finds the refugee censuses of the Russian Caucasus about 70% above the Ottoman figures for the same districts.

sentences.text: For the dead, the American Committee's bulletin of May 1916 computed “between 450,000 and 850,000” and called 600,000 safe, and Toynbee summed up that “about an equal number of Armenians in Turkey seem to have escaped, to have perished, and to have survived deportation in 1915”, each category in round numbers 600,000.
Toynbee's own convoy figures run from 18,000 at Malatia to 150 at Aleppo, and from 5,000 to 213 on the road from Harput.

By December 1916 the German administrator who had watched Erzurum emptied reported that his fear “that the evacuation of the Armenians would be tantamount to their annihilation” had come true and that the Turkish Armenians, “with the exception of several hundred thousand living in Constantinople and other larger cities, have been practically wiped out”.
The later counts, the Bundestag's, the White House's and the scholarship's spread, are set out under the disagreements below with the producers of each.

Foreign Office note just received transmits a communication requesting that it be notified urgently to Ottoman Government as follows: May 24. For about a month the Kurd and Turkish population of Armenia has been massacring Armenians with the connivance and often assistance of Ottoman authorities. Such massacres took place in middle April (new style) at Erzerum, Dertchun, Eguine, Van, Bitlis, Mush, Sassun, Zeitun, and throughout Cilicia. Inhabitants of about one hundred villages near Van were all murdered. In that city Armenian quarter is besieged by Kurds. At the same time in Constantinople Ottoman Government ill-treats inoffensive Armenian population. In view of these new crimes of Turkey against humanity and civilization, the Allied governments announce publicly to the Sublime Porte that they will hold personally responsible [for] these crimes all members of the Ottoman Government and those of their agents who are implicated in such massacres. 2 Sharp Repeated to the Ambassador in Turkey for communication in paraphrase, May 29, No. 715. ↩

sentences.text: The Allied declaration of 24 May did not use the word; it spoke of “crimes of Turkey against humanity and civilization”.

The Treaty of Sèvres of 10 August 1920 made Turkey recognise Armenia as a free and independent state, refused to recognise conversions to Islam made since 1 November 1914 in view of the “terrorist régime”, and bound the Turkish government to hand over “the persons whose surrender may be required by the latter as being responsible for the massacres”.

The Convention of 9 December 1948 defines genocide as acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”, and names among them “Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part”.

A prosecution document at Nuremberg, headed as Hitler's talk to his commanders of 22-8-39, ends a passage on killing the Polish population with the line “Who still talks nowadays of the extermination of the Armenians ?”, as the volume prints it.

On 18 June 1987 the European Parliament resolved that the events of 1915-1917 “constitute genocide within the meaning of the convention”, and in the same paragraph that “neither political nor legal or material claims against present-day Turkey can be derived from the recognition”.
Its preamble records that the Turkish state “rejects the charge of genocide as unfounded”.

The Bundestag's printed paper 18/8613, a motion as tabled, states that the planned expulsion and destruction of the Armenians began on 24 April 1915, and that the German Reich, the principal military ally, despite unambiguous information from its own diplomats and missionaries, did not try to stop it.
The President of the United States said on 24 April 2021 that “one and a half million Armenians were deported, massacred, or marched to their deaths in a campaign of extermination”.

The Republic of Armenia's declaration of independence, in its 11th article, stands in support of the international recognition of the 1915 genocide of the Armenians in Ottoman Turkey and Western Armenia.
The record holds no judgment of any court on the word, and the thesis does not supply one.

adjudications.reasoning: The German ambassador reported on 7 July 1915 that the Porte had extended the measure to Trebizond, Mamuret-ul-Aziz and Sivas although those provinces were threatened by no enemy invasion; the American ambassador reported on 10 July that the deportations were directed from Constantinople often in districts where no military operations were likely, and on 11 August that Ada Bazar, Izmid and Bardizag, some 50 miles from the capital, were being cleared; the consul at Samsun on the Black Sea reported countermeasures apparently valid for all Anatolian Vilayets and the expulsion of every Armenian there; and the German embassy's own memorandum of 9 August told the Porte it had extended the banishment order to the other provinces of Asia Minor and emptied the Armenian villages of the Izmid district. The position, stated in full, allows for some Armenians away from the front, suspected of collaboration, being included; what the ally and the neutral record is a wholesale extension to provinces and towns far from any front, not a selection of suspects. Two producers contradict the claim on that point.

My 778, June 18, 6 p. m. Persecution of Armenians assuming unprecedented proportions. Reports from widely scattered districts indicate systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations and through arbitrary arrests, terrible tortures, wholesale expulsions and deportations from one end of the Empire to the other accompanied by frequent instances of rape, pillage, and murder, turning into massacre, to bring destruction and destitution on them. These measures are not in response to popular or fanatical demand, but are purely arbitrary and directed from Constantinople in the name of military necessity, often in districts where no military operations are likely to take place. The Moslem and Armenian populations have been living in harmony, but because Armenian volunteers, many of them Russian subjects, have joined Russian Army in the Caucasus and because some have been implicated in armed revolutionary movements and others have been helpful to Russians in their invasion of Van district, terrible vengeance is being taken. Most of the sufferers are innocent and have been loyal to Ottoman Government. Nearly all are old men [and] women. All the men from 20 to 45 are in Turkish army. The victims find themselves dispossessed of their homes and sent on foot to be dispersed in districts where they are unknown, and no provisions have been made to lodge or to feed them. We have in several places been refused permission to relieve their misery or to have access to them. In some few instances where they opposed these measures and took refuge in the mountains and some arms or bombs were found, it provoked the authorities to further cruelties which they attempt to justify by the opposition. Untold misery, disease, Starvation, and loss of life will go on unchecked. Consul Davis of Harput reports: Professors American College have been tortured. Some others have died under torture or lost mind. Many hundred young Armenian men originally taken as soldiers, some of whom were students American College, have been sent away without food, clothing, or money. Night of June 23 several hundred other Armenians recently arrested, including professors American College, were sent away in the middle of the night without food, clothing, or money. Many deaths are reported en route in both lots of prisoners. Preparations are being made apparently to send away many more. I was informed confidentially to-day that an enormous sum of money is now being demanded of the local Armenians. There seems to be a systematic plan to crush the Armenian race. All things make us apprehend permanent closing of American schools. That only refers to one place. Many Armenians are becoming Moslems to avoid persecution. In addition to humanitarian considerations we have a real interest through the fact that certain objectionable Armenians involved in these forced dispossessions and deportations are naturalized citizens of the United States and that the charitable and educational work of the American Board will suffer considerably and in many places will cease altogether. The only embassy here which might assist in lessening these atrocities is the German, but I believe it will simply content itself with giving advice and a formal protest probably intended for record and to cover itself from future responsibility. German Ambassador is about to leave on a six weeks’ vacation. Have impressed on him that he and his Government will have considerable share in the odium. Immediately upon arrival of his substitute I shall make herculean efforts to enlist his sympathies. Austrian Ambassador has promised me to try to influence Minister of the Interior. I have repeatedly spoken to the Grand Vizier and pleaded earnestly with Minister of the Interior and Minister of War to stop this persecution. My arguments were unavailing except as to Constantinople. The men in authority are revolutionists and displaced the Hamidian Government with the cooperation of some Armenian revolutionists who know their method and are feared by them as a possible nucleus of a [counter-revolution?] against the present authorities. They admit that they will resort to any and every means to prevent their losing control of Government. They state that it is the Union and Progress committee’s nationalistic policy which they refused to modify even when Russia, France, and Great Britain threatened Ottoman Cabinet Ministers with personal responsibility. Turkish authorities desire to avail themselves of present conditions when three of the great powers are at war with them, Italy in strained relations, and the two others are their allies and therefore will not interfere when they are successfully defending the formidable attack at the Dardanelles. I have conferred with various American missionaries now here [from] Tajmarsovan [Marsovan?], Beirut, Bardizag, and Constantinople, and all agree that present crisis is worse than 1895 and 1896 massacres, but none of them could suggest any further steps than those I have already taken. They fear that the matter will have to run its course. Turkish authorities have definitely informed me that I have no right to interfere with their internal affairs. Still I desire to ask whether you have any suggestions. American Ambassador

My telegrams numbers 841 and 858. 1 Turkish anti-Armenian activities continue unabated. Reports, of which you will receive copies, are constantly received from our consuls and others, of horrors to which large numbers of innocent and helpless people of this race are being subjected. Armenian population is fast being swept from the Ada Bazar and Izmid. Bardizag, some 50 miles from Constantinople, has been lately threatened, but the Minister of State has granted two weeks’ delay, and unless something can be done to arrest this atrocious campaign, these people also will be forced from their homes and herded like cattle into the arid and hostile wastes of the interior, where the greater number, possibly excepting those who in desperation embrace Mohammedanism, will doubtless perish by murder or slow starvation. Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of the Interior have promised me permission for Armenians in Constantinople to leave the country on agreement never to return. Minister of the Interior says that he realizes no Armenians can remain friendly to Turkish Government after present treatment and hints at drastic measures against all in Constantinople if slightest offense is committed against Government. In view of the ease with which pretexts are created in this country, these statements cause me uneasiness. The German and Austrian Ambassadors have promised me to exert their influence, but I doubt the efficacy of their representations unless they are specifically instructed by their Governments to insist on the cessation of the acts now being perpetrated and the taking of strong protective measures for the thousands already on the way to their doom. There remain a considerable number of American missionaries at various points in the interior and though these people are prevented from rendering any adequate assistance to the Yakutsk victims and are viewed with considerable suspicion on account of their sympathies, yet I do not think they are in any personal danger now. I have this phase of riots constantly in mind and will take every measure possible for their protection and departure, should events necessitate. For the present I am inclined to think with Peet and others, that it is better for them to remain where they are in case of possible relief measures. I earnestly beg the Department to give this matter urgent and exhaustive consideration with a view to reaching a conclusion which may possibly have the effect of checking this Government and certainly provide opportunity for efficient relief which now is not permitted. It is difficult for me to restrain myself from doing something to stop this attempt to exterminate a race, but I realize that I am here as Ambassador and must abide by the principles of non-interference with the internal affairs of another country. Unless you should deem this such an exceptional state of affairs, the Department will direct me to register an unequivocal protest on behalf or our Government. I offer for serious consideration the following suggestions in the hope that they may be of assistance in reaching a conclusion in the matter which is at once urgent and delicate and further complicated by our representation of so many other foreign interests: (1) That the United States Government on behalf of humanity urgently request the Turkish Government to cease at once the present campaign and to permit the survivors to return to their homes if not in the war zones, or else to receive proper treatment; (2) That if our present relations permit, an official appeal be made to the Emperor of Germany to insist on Turkey, his ally, stopping this annihilation of a Christian race; (3) That a vigorous official demand be made without delay for the granting of every facility to Americans and others to visit and render pecuniary and other assistance they may desire to Armenians already affected by Government deportation. I believe the third suggestion might prove the most acceptable under the circumstances and that a strong and unyielding stand in this matter of our right to advance immediate aid to these helpless people will in itself imply our protesting attitude. The advance of such assistance might be the means of saving thousands during this period of the war tension, after which the situation may assume more hopeful proportions. Morgenthau Latter not printed. ↩

restsOn.text: Die getroffenen Gegenmaßregeln - anscheinend für alle anatolischen Wilajets gültig - sind jedoch von einer Härte und dem Menschlichkeitsgefühl so widerstrebend, daß sie nicht gleichgültig hingenommen werden können: Es handelt sich um nichts weniger als um die Vernichtung oder gewaltsame Islamisierung eines ganzen Volkes, dessen Angehörige zum größten Teil an der revolutionären Bewegung keinen direkten Anteil hatten, also unschuldige Opfer sind. Die Art der Ausführung des Verbannungsbefehls droht Formen anzunehmen, die nur in der Judenverfolgung Spaniens und Portugals ein Gleichnis finden: Die Regierung entsandte fanatische, strenggläubige mohamedanische Männer und Frauen in alle armenischen Häuser behufs Propaganda für den Übertritt zum Islam, selbstverständlich unter Androhung der schwersten Folgen für diejenigen, die ihrem Glauben treu bleiben. Soviel mir bekannt, sind bis heute hier schon viele Familien übergetreten und täglich vermehrt sich deren Zahl. Die Mehrheit der Unglücklichen widerstand bis jetzt den Lockungen und wurde täglich gruppenweise ins Innere getrieben. Fast keinem verblieb Zeit zur Regelung seiner Angelegenheiten. Nur mit dem Notdürftigsten versehen, mußten sie ihr Heim und Hab und Gut im Stiche lassen. Wie ich erfahre werden sie an nicht entfernten Punkten jetzt zurückgehalten, um dort noch gründlicher für den Islam bearbeitet zu werden; einige von ihnen kehrten zu diesem Zwecke auch nach hier zurück. In der Umgebung von Samsun sind alle armenischen Dörfer mohamedanisiert worden, ebenso in Uniah. Vergünstigungen wurden, ausser den Renegaten, niemandem zu Teil. Alle Armenier ohne Ausnahme: Männer, Frauen, Greise, Kinder, bis zum Säugling, Altgläubige, Protestanten und Katholiken - welch letztere sich nie einer nationalen revolutionären Bewegung anschlossen und auch von Hamid verschont wurden - mußten fort. Kein christlicher Armenier darf hier bleiben; selbst nicht solche ausländischer Staatsangehörigkeit; letztere sollen ausgewiesen werden. Der Bestimmungsort der Samsuner Verbannten ist nach Aussage des Mütessarifs Urfa.

[ Received October 16 .] My Dear Mr. Secretary : I have the honor to enclose for your confidential information a copy of a memorandum handed to the Imperial Ottoman Government by the acting Imperial Ambassador at Constantinople on August 9 about the expulsion of the Armenians. The Imperial Ottoman Government has informed the German Government that it will take the measures necessary to prevent the repetition of excesses. I am [etc.] J. Bernstorff [Enclosure—Translation] The German Embassy in Turkey to the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs Memorandum By its memorandum of July 4, the German Embassy had the honor to acquaint the Sublime Porte With the views of the Imperial German Government concerning the banishment of the Armenian inhabitants of the Anatolian provinces and to draw its attention to the fact that the measures had been attended in several places by acts of violence such as massacres and plundering which the end sought by the Ottoman Imperial Government could not justify. The German Embassy regrets to state that it appears from information received subsequently from impartial and trustworthy sources that incidents of that character, instead of being prevented by the local authorities, have regularly occurred upon the expulsion of Armenians, so that most of them perished even before reaching their destination. These are reported mainly from the provinces of Trebizond, Diarbekr and Erzerum. In some places, at Mardin for instance, all the Christians without distinction of race or faith have had the same fate. At the same time the Ottoman Imperial Government saw fit to extend the banishment order to the other provinces of Asia Minor, and quite recently the Armenian villages of the Izmid district were emptied of their inhabitants under like conditions. In the presence of those events the German Embassy, by order of its Government, is constrained to remonstrate once more upon those horrible deeds and to decline any responsibility for the consequences they may involve. It finds itself under the necessity of drawing the attention of the Ottoman Government to that point all the more as public opinion is already inclined to believe that Germany as a friendly power allied to Turkey may have approved or even instigated those acts of violence. Pera [Constantinople] , August 9, 1915 .

adjudications.claim: No authentic evidence exists to support the claim that there was a premeditated plan by the Ottoman Government to kill off Armenians.
adjudications.reasoning: The free record holds no Ottoman order to kill and no Ottoman archival file; the Ottoman archives, the interior ministry's ciphered telegrams and the 1919 court-martial verdict could not be read free, and that gap is stated in the record. What it holds is the German ambassador's report of the interior minister's own words to an embassy official, that the Porte meant to use the war to make a clean sweep of its internal enemies, and the two ambassadors' independent readings of measures directed from the capital with the eradication of the Armenians as their purpose. That is evidence of intent recorded by the ally and by a neutral, not the plan itself; the position's word authentic goes to documents this record does not hold, so the verdict stops at qualified.

restsOn.text: Ottoman Government took a number of measures for safe transfer during the relocation. However, under war-time conditions exacerbated by internal strife, local groups seeking revenge, banditry, famine, epidemics, and a failing state apparatus (including unruly officials who were court-martialed and sentenced to capital punishment by the Ottoman Government in 1916, much before the end of the War) all combined to produce what became a tragedy. Nevertheless, no authentic evidence exists to support the claim that there was a premeditated plan by the Ottoman Government to kill off Armenians. Moreover, the Ottoman socio-cultural fabric did not harbor racist attitudes that would facilitate such a horrific crime. Loss of life, regardless of numbers and regardless of possible guilt on the part of the victims, is tragic and must be remembered. However, it is factually problematic, morally unsound and legally unfounded to call this episode a “genocide.”

adjudications.reasoning: The German ambassador wrote that the transport to a destination many hundreds of kilometres away, without means of transport, through country offering neither shelter nor food and infested with typhus, was bound to claim numerous victims, and that from Erzincan the deportees were left to run the gauntlet of Kurdish bands; the American ambassador wrote that those herded into the arid and hostile wastes of the interior would doubtless perish by murder or slow starvation; the German administrator at Erzurum counted between 10 and 20,000 killed on the road to Erzincan against the government's 3 to 4,000; and the deported woman's own narrative from Moush records the company of 8,000 to 10,000 diminished by half. Three producers, the ally, a neutral and the survivors as a British ministry printed them, carry the claim.

My telegrams numbers 841 and 858. 1 Turkish anti-Armenian activities continue unabated. Reports, of which you will receive copies, are constantly received from our consuls and others, of horrors to which large numbers of innocent and helpless people of this race are being subjected. Armenian population is fast being swept from the Ada Bazar and Izmid. Bardizag, some 50 miles from Constantinople, has been lately threatened, but the Minister of State has granted two weeks’ delay, and unless something can be done to arrest this atrocious campaign, these people also will be forced from their homes and herded like cattle into the arid and hostile wastes of the interior, where the greater number, possibly excepting those who in desperation embrace Mohammedanism, will doubtless perish by murder or slow starvation. Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of the Interior have promised me permission for Armenians in Constantinople to leave the country on agreement never to return. Minister of the Interior says that he realizes no Armenians can remain friendly to Turkish Government after present treatment and hints at drastic measures against all in Constantinople if slightest offense is committed against Government. In view of the ease with which pretexts are created in this country, these statements cause me uneasiness. The German and Austrian Ambassadors have promised me to exert their influence, but I doubt the efficacy of their representations unless they are specifically instructed by their Governments to insist on the cessation of the acts now being perpetrated and the taking of strong protective measures for the thousands already on the way to their doom. There remain a considerable number of American missionaries at various points in the interior and though these people are prevented from rendering any adequate assistance to the Yakutsk victims and are viewed with considerable suspicion on account of their sympathies, yet I do not think they are in any personal danger now. I have this phase of riots constantly in mind and will take every measure possible for their protection and departure, should events necessitate. For the present I am inclined to think with Peet and others, that it is better for them to remain where they are in case of possible relief measures. I earnestly beg the Department to give this matter urgent and exhaustive consideration with a view to reaching a conclusion which may possibly have the effect of checking this Government and certainly provide opportunity for efficient relief which now is not permitted. It is difficult for me to restrain myself from doing something to stop this attempt to exterminate a race, but I realize that I am here as Ambassador and must abide by the principles of non-interference with the internal affairs of another country. Unless you should deem this such an exceptional state of affairs, the Department will direct me to register an unequivocal protest on behalf or our Government. I offer for serious consideration the following suggestions in the hope that they may be of assistance in reaching a conclusion in the matter which is at once urgent and delicate and further complicated by our representation of so many other foreign interests: (1) That the United States Government on behalf of humanity urgently request the Turkish Government to cease at once the present campaign and to permit the survivors to return to their homes if not in the war zones, or else to receive proper treatment; (2) That if our present relations permit, an official appeal be made to the Emperor of Germany to insist on Turkey, his ally, stopping this annihilation of a Christian race; (3) That a vigorous official demand be made without delay for the granting of every facility to Americans and others to visit and render pecuniary and other assistance they may desire to Armenians already affected by Government deportation. I believe the third suggestion might prove the most acceptable under the circumstances and that a strong and unyielding stand in this matter of our right to advance immediate aid to these helpless people will in itself imply our protesting attitude. The advance of such assistance might be the means of saving thousands during this period of the war tension, after which the situation may assume more hopeful proportions. Morgenthau Latter not printed. ↩

restsOn.text: 24. MOUSH DISTRICT : NARRATIVE OF A DEPORTED WOMAN, RELATED BY HER TO MR. VARTKES OF MOUSH*, RECORDED BY HIM ON THE 25th JULY, 1915, AND PUBLISHED SUBSEQUENTLY IN THE ARMENIAN JOURNAL “ VAN-TOSP.” To-day I heard a terrible story. All the Armenians who were deported from Moush were either killed or drowned in the Mourad Riverf. Among these were my mother and three sisters with their children. This news was brought to us by a woman who came here at midnight. We thought she was a ghost, as she seemed like one coming from the grave. She had saved her two-year-old boy. She immediately asked for bread. We had not any, as we were living on raw grain and meat, but we gave her what we had. After she had had enough, we asked her all kinds of questions. She was from the village of Kheiban, and was one of the deported. This is what she told us : The Turks collected all the women and children of the villages of Sordar, Pazou, Hassanova, Salekan and Gvars, and after keeping them for five days they brought them to Ziaret. Here the inhabitants of Meghd, Baghlou, Ourough, Ziaret and Kheiban joined them, and they were all taken towards the bridge over the Mourad River. On the way the families from the villages of Dorn, Hergerd, Norag, Aladin, GomsJ, Khashkhaldoukh, Souloukh, Khoronk, Kartzor, Kizil Agatch, Komer, Shekhlan, Avazaghpur, Plel and Kurdmeidan joined the party, making altogether a company of 8,000 to 10,000 people. ££ All the old women and the weak who were unable to walk vere killed. There were about one hundred Kurdish guards over us, and our lives depended on their pleasure. It was a very common thing for them to rape our girls in our presence. Very often they violated eight or ten-year-old girls, and as a consequence many would be unable to walk, and were shot. Our company moved on slowly, leaving heaps of corpses behind. Most of us were almost naked. When we passed by a village, all the Kurdish men and women would come and rob us as they pleased. When a Kurd fancied a girl, nothing would prevent him from taking her. The babies of those who were carried away were killed in our presence. They gave us bread once every other day, though many did not get even that. When all our provisions were gone, we gathered wheat from the fields and ate it. Many a mother lost her mind and dropped her baby by the wayside.

restsOn.text: The Armenian Genocide involves a combination of the above acts. During World War I, mass murder, deportation, and forced assimilation were three faces of the same process of destruction organized by the Young Turk regime. The main objective of the whole process was to demographically reduce the Ottoman Armenian community from existence to absence as well as erasing their material and cultural presence from the Ottoman heartland and eastern provinces. Whereas Armenian men were mostly perished in the eastern provinces, Armenian women and children were most often deported and absorbed into Muslim households. After enduring forced marches where they were terrorized and forced to bear witness to the execution of their elders, these young women and children were left isolated from their families and were thus deemed prime candidates for absorption into Muslim households, 2 a process referred to as “conversion.”

adjudications.claim: The Ottoman ministers made no particular attempt to conceal, in their conversations with the ambassador, that the deportation was the death warrant of a race.
adjudications.reasoning: The ambassador's own telegrams of 1915 record the Grand Vizier resenting foreign interference and the ministers justifying the measures on the ground of military necessity, which is concealment rather than candour; the German record carries the interior minister's blunt words to an embassy official, that the Porte would use the war to make a clean sweep of its internal enemies. The memoir's claim is borne out by the German file and not by the ambassador's own contemporaneous file, so the verdict is qualified: candour to the German embassy, pretext to the American.

Your 715 communicated on June 3 to the Grand Vizier who expressed regret at being held personally responsible and resentment at attempted interference by foreign governments with the sovereign rights of the Turkish Government over their Armenian subjects. restsOn.text: File No. 867.4016/74 The Ambassador in Turkey ( Morgenthau ) to the Secretary of State [Telegram] Constantinople , July 10, 1915, 9 a. m. [ Received July 14, 10.20 a. m. ] 841. My 778, June 18, 6 p. m. Persecution of Armenians assuming unprecedented proportions. Reports from widely scattered districts indicate systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations and through arbitrary arrests, terrible tortures, wholesale expulsions and deportations from one end of the Empire to the other accompanied by frequent instances of rape, pillage, and murder, turning into massacre, to bring destruction and destitution on them. These measures are not in response to popular or fanatical demand, but are purely arbitrary and directed from Constantinople in the name of military necessity, often in districts where no military operations are likely to take place. The Moslem and Armenian populations have been living in harmony, but because Armenian volunteers, many of them Russian subjects, have joined Russian Army in the Caucasus and because some have been implicated in armed revolutionary movements and others have been helpful to Russians in their invasion of Van district, terrible vengeance is being taken. Most of the sufferers are innocent and have been loyal to Ottoman Government. Nearly all are old men [and] women. All the men from 20 to 45 are in Turkish army. The victims find themselves dispossessed of their homes and sent on foot to be dispersed in districts where they are unknown, and no provisions have been made to lodge or to feed them. We have in several places been refused permission to relieve their misery or to have access to them. In some few instances where they opposed these measures and took refuge in the mountains and some arms or bombs were found, it provoked the authorities to further cruelties which they attempt to justify by the opposition. Untold misery, disease, Starvation, and loss of life will go on unchecked. Consul Davis of Harput reports: Professors American College have been tortured. Some others have died under torture or lost mind. Many hundred young Armenian men originally taken as soldiers, some of whom were students American College, have been sent away without food, clothing, or money. Night of June 23 several hundred other Armenians recently arrested, including professors American College, were sent away in the middle of the night without food, clothing, or money. Many deaths are reported en route in both lots of prisoners. Preparations are being made apparently to send away many more. I was informed confidentially to-day that an enormous sum of money is now being demanded of the local Armenians. There seems to be a systematic plan to crush the Armenian race. All things make us apprehend permanent closing of American schools. That only refers to one place. Many Armenians are becoming Moslems to avoid persecution. In addition to humanitarian considerations we have a real interest through the fact that certain objectionable Armenians involved in these forced dispossessions and deportations are naturalized citizens of the United States and that the charitable and educational work of the American Board will suffer considerably and in many places will cease altogether. The only embassy here which might assist in lessening these atrocities is the German, but I believe it will simply content itself with giving advice and a formal protest probably intended for record and to cover itself from future responsibility. German Ambassador is about to leave on a six weeks’ vacation. Have impressed on him that he and his Government will have considerable share in the odium. Immediately upon arrival of his substitute I shall make herculean efforts to enlist his sympathies. Austrian Ambassador has promised me to try to influence Minister of the Interior. I have repeatedly spoken to the Grand Vizier and pleaded earnestly with Minister of the Interior and Minister of War to stop this persecution. My arguments were unavailing except as to Constantinople. The men in authority are revolutionists and displaced the Hamidian Government with the cooperation of some Armenian revolutionists who know their method and are feared by them as a possible nucleus of a [counter-revolution?] against the present authorities. They admit that they will resort to any and every means to prevent their losing control of Government. They state that it is the Union and Progress committee’s nationalistic policy which they refused to modify even when Russia, France, and Great Britain threatened Ottoman Cabinet Ministers with personal responsibility. Turkish authorities desire to avail themselves of present conditions when three of the great powers are at war with them, Italy in strained relations, and the two others are their allies and therefore will not interfere when they are successfully defending the formidable attack at the Dardanelles. I have conferred with various American missionaries now here [from] Tajmarsovan [Marsovan?], Beirut, Bardizag, and Constantinople, and all agree that present crisis is worse than 1895 and 1896 massacres, but none of them could suggest any further steps than those I have already taken. They fear that the matter will have to run its course. Turkish authorities have definitely informed me that I have no right to interfere with their internal affairs. Still I desire to ask whether you have any suggestions. American Ambassador

adjudications.claim: Germany, the Ottoman Empire's ally, protested and did not stop the deportations.
adjudications.reasoning: The German embassy's memoranda of 4 July and 9 August 1915 are in the American file, sent by the German ambassador in Washington; the German ambassador at Constantinople wrote that he handed the first to the Grand Vizier to answer later accusations of complicity; by December 1916 his own consul reported the Turkish Armenians as good as wiped out outside the large cities; and the Bundestag's resolution of 2016 states that the Reich did not try to stop it. [ Received October 16 .] My Dear Mr. Secretary : I have the honor to enclose for your confidential information a copy of a memorandum handed to the Imperial Ottoman Government by the acting Imperial Ambassador at Constantinople on August 9 about the expulsion of the Armenians. The Imperial Ottoman Government has informed the German Government that it will take the measures necessary to prevent the repetition of excesses. I am [etc.] J. Bernstorff [Enclosure—Translation] The German Embassy in Turkey to the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs Memorandum By its memorandum of July 4, the German Embassy had the honor to acquaint the Sublime Porte With the views of the Imperial German Government concerning the banishment of the Armenian inhabitants of the Anatolian provinces and to draw its attention to the fact that the measures had been attended in several places by acts of violence such as massacres and plundering which the end sought by the Ottoman Imperial Government could not justify. The German Embassy regrets to state that it appears from information received subsequently from impartial and trustworthy sources that incidents of that character, instead of being prevented by the local authorities, have regularly occurred upon the expulsion of Armenians, so that most of them perished even before reaching their destination. These are reported mainly from the provinces of Trebizond, Diarbekr and Erzerum. In some places, at Mardin for instance, all the Christians without distinction of race or faith have had the same fate. At the same time the Ottoman Imperial Government saw fit to extend the banishment order to the other provinces of Asia Minor, and quite recently the Armenian villages of the Izmid district were emptied of their inhabitants under like conditions. In the presence of those events the German Embassy, by order of its Government, is constrained to remonstrate once more upon those horrible deeds and to decline any responsibility for the consequences they may involve. It finds itself under the necessity of drawing the attention of the Ottoman Government to that point all the more as public opinion is already inclined to believe that Germany as a friendly power allied to Turkey may have approved or even instigated those acts of violence. Pera [Constantinople] , August 9, 1915 .

adjudications.claim: The tragic events in 1915-1917 involving the Armenians living in the territory of the Ottoman Empire constitute genocide within the meaning of the Convention.

sentences.text: The state's position is held here in its own words, from its pamphlet of 1916 to its foreign ministry's page, which calls the Armenian narrative one that “selects the Armenian suffering, embellishes it in several ways and presents it as a genocide” and holds that “greater numbers of Turks died or were killed in the years leading to and during the War”.

Its strongest line is Rüstem's, that the survival of hundreds of thousands of Ottoman Armenians proves there was no extermination, and the German record answers it in its own terms: the officer who had reported from Erzurum wrote in December 1916 that the Turkish Armenians, “with the exception of several hundred thousand living in Constantinople and other larger cities, have been practically wiped out”.

The witnesses' position is the memoir's, that the deportation was “a new method of massacre” and the ministers “made no particular attempt to conceal the fact”, and the memoir's Talaat says “we have already disposed of three quarters of the” Armenians; the editor of the minister's own report prints the diary's version, “they had already disposed of three quarters of them”.

The scholarship held here calls mass murder, deportation and forced assimilation “three faces of the same process of destruction organized by the Young Turk regime”, describes conversion as a bureaucratic process from Talat Pasha's own directives, and gives the spread of estimates of the dead as running upward from 800,000.

Kévorkian's survey, in French, records that the Interior Ministry's fonds opened in 2005 show the administrative planning of the deportations and a will to transform the composition of Asia Minor, and that survivor testimony was long denied the standing of the state's own documents.

The Armenian scholarship held here reports the court-martial's death sentences of 5 July 1919 on Talât, Enver, Cemal and Nazım, 20 death sentences in 63 cases and 3 carried out, and the law's position is the French parliament's bill of 18 January 2001 and the parliaments' resolutions above.
